key_insight: The paper demonstrates that several dialectal varieties of Nawatl can be automatically distinguished despite limited digital resources and inconsistent orthography, using a targeted collection and classification approach optimized for low-resource, dialect-rich languages.
problem_solved: Addresses automatic identification and classification of multiple Nawatl dialects when digital corpora are scarce and written forms vary widely across regions and speakers.
method: Assemble and annotate a multi-dialect Nawatl corpus that captures regional varieties and spelling variation.
Preprocess and normalize orthographic variants and extract linguistically informed features (lexical, morphological, or embeddings) suitable for dialect discrimination.
Train and evaluate supervised classification models (including resource-efficient or transfer-learning strategies) with cross-dialect validation and error analysis to identify confusable pairs.
impact: Provides a practical blueprint for building dialect-aware NLP tools for low-resource, indigenous languages; enables better documentation, search, and language technologies that respect regional variation.
visual_elements: Map of Mexico/Central America with annotated dialect regions and relative speaker density for each Nawatl variety.
Pipeline diagram showing steps: data collection → orthographic normalization → feature extraction → classifier → evaluation.
Confusion-matrix heatmap highlighting which dialect pairs are most frequently confused by the model.
Bar/stacked chart summarizing dataset composition (samples per dialect, proportions of orthographic variants) and overall classifier accuracy.
paper_authors: Juan-José Guzmán-Landa, Juan-Manuel Torres-Moreno, Miguel Figueroa-Saavedra, Carlos-Emiliano González-Gallardo, Graham Ranger
